newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ABB CEO says forecast sets floor.
newsitem.headline: ABB CEO says forecast sets floor.

text.p: Goran Lindahl, president and chief executive of ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG said his forecast for 1997 net profit to at least reach the 1996 level should be viewed as minimum for what profit he expects to reach.
Lindahl also told Reuters in a telephone interview that he was satisfied with the first quarter results, especially the order intake, which he said was "promising for the future".

"It's a result that we are satisfied with and if you compare with a comparable basis, including the currencies, then it is a good increase, especially I would underline the order intake that is promising for the future. We will be able to add to order backlog, that is always good," Lindahl said.
ABB earlier reported a 16 percent increase in new orders for the first quarter of 1997 to $10.08 billion. In local currencies, the increase amounted to 22 percent.
ABB's net profit rose eight percent to $236 million and in local currencies the rise amounted to 14 percent.
For the full year, ABB repeated that it expects net income to "reach at least the same level as in 1996."
"This is definitely a floor and no ceiling whatsoever," Lindahl said when asked about the forecast.
ABB reported a 1996 group net profit of $1,233 million, an increase of 16 percent on a comparable basis.
Lindahl said his profit forecast was "still a cautious outlook," noting ABB was still in the second year of a downturn in Europe and a pickup in demand would first come next year.

"It is very uncertain whether it comes before," Lindahl said about a demand pull from Europe, adding there was a great deal of uncertainty in Europe linked with the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the huge unemployment problem.
"I must be fair to the markets and say I have no crystal ball and cannot say exactly what happens here and that's why I established a floor, but I have some confidence in that floor," he said.
Referring to the first quarter results, Lindahl noted a stronger U.S. dollar had a negative effect of six percent on ABB's operating and net results.
The stronger dollar this year had a negative effect when European currencies are translated into dollars, the currency that ABB reports in.
Net profit as reported rose eight percent, but in local currencies the rise amounted to 14 percent, Lindahl noted.
To help compensate for the weakness in Europe, Lindahl said ABB was increasing its sales efforts to increase market penetration and thus boost business volume.
"In our case we go for selective volume that can positively contribute to our bottom line," he said.
Another push is in the service and revamping business, where Lindahl said he still wants to double sales by year 2000 or 2001 from last year's $six billion.
In both sales and service ABB is now increasing its staffing levels, Lindahl said, and this should "continue to give a good outcome in orders received."

A slight decline in first quarter operating earnings at ABB's Industrial and Building Systems segment was mainly due to a shortfall in standard products, Lindahl said, noting this was a continuation of the trend seen in the latter part of 1996.
The Power Generation segment was also benefiting from recent restructuring, but Lindahl declined to specify this on a quarterly basis.

"We see a gradual positive impact of restructuring and that will continue through this year before we have the full impact," Lindahl said, adding this issue would be addressed next year, when looking back at 1997.

Lindahl said he was not concerned about a drop in ABB's cash position at the end of the first quarter, attributing this to lower advance payments and also a build-up in inventories ahead of the billing of large projects next quarter.
"Our ambition to have an increase in net cash position stands and for the full year we will report a better result there," he said.
-- Peter Nielsen, Zurich Editorial +41 1 631
